summary:
Corse stands under the national framework of France. French law on identity documents, criminal procedure, anti-discrimination, marriage and criminal law applies uniformly across metropolitan and overseas regions, and no Corse-specific finding on transgender detainees, border checks or hate violence appears in the sources; the national mechanisms documented below apply on the island unchanged.

Detention is the setting where the risk is documented most concretely. Article D248 of the Criminal Procedure Code mandates separate establishments for men and women, so placement follows the sex inscribed on identity documents and trans women are typically held in men's facilities. As of 1 November 2016 there were 13 transgender detainees held across eight establishments, most of them at Fleury-Mérogis. Each facility improvises within that rule, using special units or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates.

A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 profiles Paola, an Argentine trans woman transferred to a men's facility in 2014, where she was met with shouts of "We don't want any women here" despite a passport listing her as female, because French law does not recognise her Argentine legal gender for placement purposes. The same reporting documents inconsistent access to treatment and a 2,000-euro symbolic damages award over detention conditions, with the justice minister pressed to amend Article D248.

The Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL), France's national preventive mechanism, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the care of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, building on referrals received since 2010 and a 2010 opinion on transsexual prisoners. Inspections cited include Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station, with evidence from eight transgender women. The opinion documents discrimination, stigmatisation and health and social-care blind spots, and recommends policies to combat the discrimination and exclusion they face, referencing law n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016 on justice modernisation and prison transfers and the "racism, antisemitism, LGBT and discrimination" referents appointed since 2018. The CGLPL reports persistent serious violations of trans detainees' rights across the prisons it inspected.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.
tangentialFactors:
The national preventive mechanism explained to the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

In everyday movement, accommodation and services, France's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition. The Défenseur des droits' framework decision and the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey figure of 64% identity-related discrimination indicate a general climate of hostility that a trans visitor may encounter outside the detention and border settings.
localsOnly:
Prison placement follows no statutory rule beyond Article D248. Where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments, and accounts collected in the BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

The CGLPL examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010, together with ministry and association input, and issued its opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations: placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure during strip searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Corse-specific finding on transgender detainees, border checks or hate violence appears in the sources; the national mechanisms documented above are stated to apply on the island unchanged, but this is an inference from the uniformity of French national law rather than a sourced Corse record.

The sources do not resolve whether Article D248 has been amended following the justice minister's being pressed to do so, nor whether the CGLPL's binding guidance of 25 May 2021 has been implemented in practice. The current placement rule as applied in Corse's detention facilities is not separately sourced.
